questions.stem: Two heterozygous brown mice (Bb) are crossed. Using a Punnett square, what is the expected ratio of brown (B_) to white (bb) offspring?
questions.explanation: Crossing Bb x Bb gives: BB (brown), Bb (brown), Bb (brown), bb (white). The genotypic ratio is 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb. Since BB and Bb both show the dominant brown phenotype, the phenotypic ratio is 3 brown : 1 white. This classic 3:1 ratio is the hallmark of a monohybrid cross between two heterozygous parents.

questions.stem: A couple are both carriers of cystic fibrosis (Cc). They have four children. What is the probability that their NEXT child will have cystic fibrosis?

options.text: 0%, because three of four children will statistically be unaffected
25%, because each pregnancy is an independent event
50%, because one parent must pass on the recessive allele
It depends on how many of their existing children have cystic fibrosis

questions.explanation: Each pregnancy is an independent genetic event. The Punnett square for Cc x Cc always gives a 1 in 4 (25%) chance of cc (affected) for each child, regardless of the outcomes of previous children. Common misconception: if three children are unaffected, the fourth is not 'due' to have cystic fibrosis - each child independently has a 25% chance.

questions.stem: A homozygous dominant red flower (RR) is crossed with a homozygous recessive white flower (rr). All F1 offspring are red (Rr). If two F1 plants are crossed, what fraction of the F2 offspring are expected to be homozygous?
questions.explanation: Crossing Rr x Rr in the F2 generation gives: RR, Rr, Rr, rr. The homozygous offspring are RR (1/4) and rr (1/4), totalling 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2 (or 2/4) homozygous. The other half (2/4) are heterozygous (Rr). Note the question asks about homozygous (both dominant and recessive), not just one type.

questions.stem: A farmer crosses a tall pea plant with a short pea plant. All offspring are tall. The farmer then crosses two of these tall offspring. In a batch of 80 F2 plants, approximately how many would be expected to be short?
questions.explanation: Since all F1 offspring are tall, the tall parent must be homozygous dominant (TT) and short is homozygous recessive (tt). F1 are all Tt. Crossing Tt x Tt gives a 3:1 ratio, so 1/4 of F2 should be short (tt). 1/4 of 80 = 20 short plants. In practice, actual numbers may vary slightly from the expected ratio due to chance.

questions.stem: In a cross between a heterozygous black guinea pig (Bb) and a white guinea pig (bb), what proportion of offspring would you expect to be white?
questions.explanation: The Punnett square for Bb x bb gives: Bb, Bb, bb, bb. That is 2 black (Bb) and 2 white (bb), giving a 1:1 phenotypic ratio. So 1/2 (50%) of offspring are expected to be white. This is different from the 3:1 ratio seen when crossing two heterozygous parents - the ratio depends on the specific parental genotypes.
